extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly — practical scientists, inventors, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and explanatory articles for a general educated readership on practical topics (personal safety such as drowning prevention) and professional/legal developments (intellectual property and technical advances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tread or walk the water (primary drowning-avoidance technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: To escape drowning it is only necessary to do as the brute does, and that is to tread or walk the water — striking alternately, one two, one two, but without hurry or precipitation, with hand and foot, exactly as the brute does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hands and feet (or feet alone / hands alone / all four) alternately and calmly; the paddle-formed human hand and ability to float give additional safety. Maintain an unhurried alternating stroke 'one two, one two' as animals do. Practicing treading water daily will make it available instinctively in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Float when tired
rubrics_metrics.description: When exhausted, escape by floating: lying quite still, with the mouth shut and the head thrown well back in the water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Floating allows rest in the water — the author cites Bridget Money saving herself and three children by floating. The ability to float is simpler than many think and is an essential complement to treading water ('Float when you are tired').

rubrics_metrics.name: Anyone who can walk can learn to tread water immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Every child or adult who can walk on land may also walk in the water, just as readily as animals do, without any prior instruction or drilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume swimming lessons are prerequisite for survival: instinctive or minimally instructed treading/ walking the water suffices in many cases. The article repeatedly emphasizes that terror and ignorance, not lack of physical capacity, account for many drownings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice treading in controlled shallow tanks (school/house recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every school and every house ought to have a slate tank of sufficient depth (with a trickle of water at one end and a siphon at the other) so each child, from when it can walk, should be made to tread water daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep contents pure by trickle and siphon; a pail or two of hot water can warm the tank. Posters/pasted injunctions should be placed at boathouses, boats, bathing-places, and schools reading 'Tread water when you find yourself out of your depth' (and optionally 'Float when you are tired').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid panic; calmness is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheer terror incapacitates people in the water and is a major reason men perish while animals survive; calm, composed action (treading or floating) preserves life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction and repeated practice reduce panic. Public education and signage are recommended to counteract terror-induced fatal reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treading water works even with clothing and in breaking seas
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone, of whatever age or sex, however encumbered with clothing, might tread water with at least as much facility — even in a breaking sea — as a four-footed animal does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume clothing makes treading impossible; encourage confidence that treading is broadly applicable under varied conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating/treading is safer and more sustainable than sprawling ordinary swimming
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of a person who treads water is, in other respects, very much safer and better than the sprawling attitude assumed in ordinary swimming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treading allows the possibility of rest by floating; ordinary swim strokes often fatigue and lead to peril. Encourage treading/ floating as primary survival techniques rather than emphasis on complex swim strokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-mark scope (legal standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade-marks cannot be classified with inventions or writings under the constitutional power that secures authors and inventors; if sustained, a federal trade-mark law must be limited to marks intended for foreign (or Indian) commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress passed (March 3, 1881) an act authorizing registration and protection only in foreign (and Indian) commerce. Practitioners should treat trade-mark legislation as distinct from patent/copyright protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-keeping systems: copyright vs patent boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: A new system of book-keeping embodied in a book of forms/blank pages with headings was held to be copyrightable only as to the introductory essay and the particular printed columns/headings as samples; to secure control of the system itself, one should seek a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject-matter is essentially a method or system rather than a literary work, patent protection may be the appropriate route. Conversely, a tangible 'book' that is a novel mechanical arrangement may be patentable (illustrated by the blank-book (bond/coupon) example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patent office classification and Gazette to survey state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office classification arranges inventions into 24 divisions, 164 classes, and nearly 3,000 subclasses; persons wishing to inform themselves about the state of the art should procure specifications and drawings in the relevant subclass or subscribe to the Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consulting specifications/drawings in the appropriate subclass is recommended for novelty searches and understanding prior art; Congress appropriated funds to prepare a digest to aid examiners and applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use and disclosure: when disclosure/ use impairs rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may use his invention openly to test its operation, ascertain defects, and mature improvements without losing his right if the use was for experiment and not for profit; however, sale or manufacture for sale (even small private sales) can constitute abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: Nicholson pavement experiment did not abandon right; making and selling finished articles to be worn out by acquaintances was held to be abandonment. Even a single sale 'on trial' can be fatal. Inventors should keep commercial exploitation distinct from experimental public uses until protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy obligations: practical measures required to avoid abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Conducting business in a way that gives the public opportunity to know and imitate the invention forfeits rights; limited numbers of workmen and locked doors without formal pledge of secrecy may be insufficient to preserve secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any person learns the invention under circumstances that would permit public disclosure without breach of confidence, the right may be considered abandoned. Employers should secure formal confidentiality commitments where secrecy is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in applying may lead to abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Although no fixed statutory time may limit application, courts have held that long neglect without good excuse (sickness, poverty, etc.) can lead to a patent being annulled for abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Woodbury case (long delay from 1848 to 1870) is cited; inventors should be vigilant and active in applying for patents and avoid undue postponement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process patents are lawful but must describe means adequately
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be granted for a process (a new and useful art of manufacture), not limited to machines or compositions; the discoverer must fully and accurately specify the means by which the useful result is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the mode of applying the process is obvious to a person skilled in the art, pointing out the process and one mode is sufficient; if not obvious, describe a particular mode or apparatus so as to show capability of actual use. The inventor need not describe every possible mode if the process is susceptible of multiple applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of process patent may reach imported products (English decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: An English Court of Appeal decided that a patent for a process includes a monopoly of the sale in England of products made according to that process abroad, because importing those products is an indirect use of the patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holders should be aware of the risk of foreign manufacturers underselling and the potential judicial support (in England) for treating importation of goods made by a patented process as infringement. Jurisdictional law may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and usefulness required — courts invalidate trivial patents
rubrics_metrics.description: To be sustained, a patent must be for something 'new and useful'; courts have invalidated patents for trivial devices which do not meet the novelty/invention standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: 'Perfection Window-Cleaner' (rubber on a handle), 'Improved Kindling-Wood' (bundles with combustible lump), fare-box additions (second window/reflector), 'Whip-Tips' socket idea (only screw patentable), 'Rubber-tip Pencil' (piece of rubber with a hole), 'Comminuted Glue' (grinding glue). Inventors should apply strict novelty tests before incurring patenting costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and frank disclosure requirement in patent specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must frankly and fully disclose his invention; Justice Clifford listed three reasons: (1) Government must know what it has granted and what becomes public property later; (2) licensees must know how to practice the invention; (3) subsequent inventors must know the remaining field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient description may be corrected by reissue only in limited circumstances. Applicants should ensure completeness and accuracy to satisfy statutory/public policy goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue is limited to correcting inadvertence, accident, or mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue may correct accidental or mistaken insufficiencies in the original patent description, but cannot be used to reclaim or add matter deliberately omitted or surrendered in the original prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court condemns reissues that effectively enlarge what the inventor earlier consented to abandon; reissue privilege has been abused and must not be used to recover previously rejected or voluntarily omitted claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use of patented inventions requires compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the American view a patent is property and government use is not a defense; when Government officers adopt a patented invention they may be held to pay damages (as if infringers) or the owner may obtain compensation via the Court of Claims on an implied contract theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: army cartridge-box inventor refused pay by War Department; Postmaster of New York City had to pay damages for using a patented postage-stamp canceling device that saved the Government money. Practitioners should seek explicit agreements or expect remedies through courts/Congressional appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt machinery (prime movers) for economical electricity generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric lighting has advanced chiefly by substituting machinery (generators driven by engines or turbines) for expensive batteries, reducing coal required per horsepower and making electricity cheaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gas-engines, water turbines, and caloric-engines are all practical sources depending on local conditions (gas-engine used at docks, water turbines used by Armstrong, caloric-engine suitable for isolated lighthouses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer small machines joined in multiple arc for efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials (e.g., for Trinity House) show more efficiency by joining small machines in multiple arc than by using a larger machine or joining the same small machines in series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting machine configuration (multiple small machines vs one large) should consider the required light characteristics and generator performance; Siemens and Gramme types convert high percentages of power to useful current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pure, large-dimension copper conductors and overhead routing when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: For conducting wires preference is given to the purest copper available and wire of the largest dimensions consistent with economy to keep resistance low and avoid waste of energy; when carried overhead, radiation of heat keeps wire cool and improves current conveyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because arc-light currents are thousands of times larger than telegraph currents, conductor sizing and routing are critical. Overhead routing aids cooling; inductive disturbances are serious and raise concerns about placing electric-light and telegraph circuits close together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match generator characteristics to the lighting task
rubrics_metrics.description: Different machines are adapted to particular work by variations in velocity or winding that produce current variations suited to the particular light required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the difference in value among good machines is not great, match machine design (Siemens, Gramme, etc.) to the specific application for best economy and performance; small machines may be economical for some installations.
